name.text: Module 2 · Lesson 7 · Section 1: Review of Lessons 5–6

questiontext.text:
Section 1: Review of Lessons 5–6

Quick Summary

In Lessons 5 and 6, we expanded our vocabulary exponentially by learning how Semitic roots generate new meanings through derived stems. The Aphel stem (prefix ʾa-) generates causative verbs (e.g., God ʾaḥī “gave life”, ʾaqreb “brought near”). The Paael stem (doubled middle radical) generates intensive or factitive verbs (e.g., qaddeš “he made holy”, ʾallep “he taught”).

5-Question Warm-Up Drill

(Answers in Section 9)

  1. What stem does a verb belonging to the pattern ʾaCCeC belong to (e.g., ʾaqreb)?
  2. What consonant prefix marks the active participle of all derived stems (Aphel, Paael, etc.)?
  3. Translate: ʾAlāhā ʾawdaʿ šrārā (ܐܠܗܐ ܐܘܕܥ ܫܪܪܐ).
  4. If q-d-š in Peal means “to be holy”, what does it mean in Paael (qaddeš)?
  5. How would you recognize a Paael participle versus a Peal participle?
Warm-up 1. A verb of the pattern ʾaCCeC (e.g. ʾaqreb) belongs to which stem?

feedback.text: The Paael doubles the middle letter and has no ʾa-.

questiontext.text: Warm-up 2. Which consonant prefix marks the active participle of every derived stem?
Warm-up 3. Translate: ʾAlāhā ʾawdaʿ šrārā.
Warm-up 4. If q-d-š in the Peal means 'to be holy', what does the Paael qaddeš mean?

feedback.text: The Paael here is factitive, not just intensive.

answer.text: to cause to be holy through another

feedback.text: That would be the causative Aphel.

questiontext.text: Warm-up 5. How do you tell a Paael participle from a Peal participle?

answer.text: The Paael has the m- prefix (mqaddeš); the Peal has none (kāteb).
The Peal has the m- prefix; the Paael has none.
The Paael ends in -ā; the Peal does not.
They look the same; only context tells.

name.text: Module 2 · Lesson 7 · Section 2: The Weak Verb Challenge — Overview

questiontext.text:
Section 2: The Weak Verb Challenge — Overview

Until now, we have mostly dealt with “strong” roots (like k-t-b or š-b-q), where all three consonants boldly assert themselves in every conjugation. However, some of the most common verbs in human language—to say, to be, to know, to give, to come—are “weak”. This means one of their three root consonants is a “weak letter” (Alaph, Waw, or Yodh, and in first position also Nun), which tends to assimilate, drop out entirely, or turn into a vowel depending on the surrounding sounds. You have been reading several of these verbs since Lesson 3 (ʾemar, ʾezal, qām, ʾappeq); this lesson explains them.

Cross-Linguistic Comparison: Weak Consonants

Weak verbs are the bane of every Semitic language student, but they follow highly predictable phonetic rules.

  • Hebrew: I-Guttural (אָמַר ʾāmar = he said); I-Yod (יָדַע yādaʿ = he knew); Lamed-He/Yod (בָּנָה bānāh = he built).
  • Arabic: Hollow verbs (قَالَ qāla = he said); Defective/Final Weak (رَمَى ramā = he threw).
  • Syriac:
    • I-Alaph: Root ʾ-m-r (to say) → ʾemar (not ʾamar).
    • I-Yodh: Root y-d-ʿ (to know) → ʾīdaʿ (Yodh acts like an ī vowel).
    • III-Yodh: Root ḥ-z-y (to see) → ḥzā (the Yodh drops out, leaving an ā vowel).
    • Hollow (II-Waw/Yodh): Root q-w-m (to rise) → qām (the middle letter disappears into a long vowel).
    • I-Nun: Root n-p-q (to go out) → imperfect neppūq, Aphel ʾappeq (the Nun assimilates to the next consonant).

name.text: Module 2 · Lesson 7 · Section 3: Morphology of Weak Roots (Peal Perfect)

questiontext.text:
Section 3: Morphology of Weak Roots (Peal Perfect)

Despite the spelling changes, weak verbs function syntactically exactly like strong verbs: VSO word order, taking suffixes, and forming the spine of clauses.

1. I-Alaph Verbs (First consonant is Alaph)

The most famous is ʾ-m-r (“to say”). In the Peal perfect 3rd masc singular, the vowel shifts to e:

  • ʾemar (he said), rather than ʾamar.
  • ʾemret (I said), rather than ʾamret.

2. I-Yodh Verbs (First consonant is Yodh)

Very common verbs like y-d-ʿ (to know) and y-t-b (to sit). A Syriac word cannot begin with a vowelless y, so the initial Yodh is pronounced as the vowel ī. Where the first radical has a vowel of its own (1 c.sg. and 3 f.sg.), it is a normal consonant again: yedʿet (I knew), yedʿat (she knew).

  • y-d-ʿ → ʾīdaʿ (he knew).
  • y-t-b → ʾīteb (he sat). Note: The verb y-h-b (to give) is irregular: in the perfect ܝܗܒ the He is written but silent, ya(h)b “he gave” (pronounced yab), 1 c.sg. yehbet “I gave”. Its imperfect is supplied by another root altogether: ܢܬܠ nettel “he will give”.

3. III-Yodh Verbs (Third consonant is Yodh)

Verbs ending in Yodh (like ḥ-z-y, b-n-y, ḥ-y-y). The Yodh falls away in the 3rd masc singular, leaving a final ā vowel. In other persons, the Yodh can reappear as heavily vocalized endings.

  • ḥ-z-y (to see) → ḥzā (he saw) [looks like a 2-consonant word].
  • ḥ-z-y + -et (I saw) → ḥzēt (the ay contracts to ē).
  • ḥ-z-y + -w (They saw) → ḥzaw (here the plural Waw is heard, as the diphthong aw).

4. Hollow Verbs (Second consonant is Waw or Yodh)

In roots like q-w-m (rise, stand), d-w-n (judge) and s-y-m (put), the middle radical is not a real consonant. In the Peal perfect it vanishes into a long ā that never changes: qām (he rose), qāmat (she rose), qāmet (I rose). The active participle shows a glottal stop or y in its place: ܩܐܡ qāʾem, f. ܩܝܡܐ qāymā. The imperfect and imperative show the long vowel of the root: ܢܩܘܡ nqūm (he will rise), ܩܘܡ qūm (rise!); for s-y-m, ܢܣܝܡ nsīm.

In the Aphel the middle radical appears as ī: ܐܩܝܡ ʾaqīm (he raised up), participle ܡܩܝܡ mqīm; likewise ʾarīm (he exalted), from r-w-m.

5. I-Nun Verbs (First consonant is Nun)

The perfect of a I-Nun verb is regular: npaq (he went out), npal (he fell), nsab (he took). But wherever the Nun would stand directly before the second radical with no vowel between them, it assimilates to that radical and doubles it:

  • Imperfect: n- + npūq → ܢܦܘܩ neppūq (he will go out); ܢܦܠ neppel (he will fall); ܢܣܒ nessab (he will take).
  • Imperative: the Nun is dropped altogether: ܦܘܩ pūq (go out!), ܣܒ sab (take!).
  • Infinitive: ܡܦܩ meppaq (to go out).
  • Aphel: ܐܦܩ ʾappeq (he brought out), participle ܡܦܩ mappeq. This is the verb you learned in Lesson 5.

Two other verbs assimilate a first or second radical in the same way: s-l-q (go up; Aphel ʾasseq, “bring up”) and ʾ-z-l (go; ʾezzet is heard for ʾezlet, “I went”).

Section 5: Hollow Paradigm; the Irregular Verbs ʾ-t-y and h-w-y

The Hollow Peal (Root q-w-m “to rise, stand”)

Form Estrangela Transliteration Translation
Perfect 3 m.sg. ܩܡ qām he rose
Perfect 3 f.sg. ܩܡܬ qāmat she rose
Perfect 2 m.sg. ܩܡܬ qāmt you (m) rose
Perfect 1 c.sg. ܩܡܬ qāmet I rose
Perfect 3 m.pl. ܩܡܘ qām(w) they (m) rose
Perfect 2 m.pl. ܩܡܬܘܢ qāmtūn you (m.pl) rose
Participle m.sg. ܩܐܡ qāʾem rising, standing
Participle f.sg. ܩܝܡܐ qāymā rising, standing

Aphel participle ܡܩܝܡ mqīm raising up

Two Doubly Weak Verbs

Two of the most common verbs in Syriac are doubly weak and highly irregular.

  1. ʾ-t-y (to come): I-Alaph AND III-Yodh.
    • 3 m.s: ʾetā (he came).
    • 1 c.s: ʾetēt (I came).
    • 3 m.pl: ʾetaw (they came).
  2. h-w-y (to be/become): Used as an auxiliary verb, or to mean “it happened”. III-Yodh.
    • 3 m.s: hwā (he was / it happened).
    • 1 c.s: hwēt (I was).
    • 3 m.pl: hwaw (they were).

The Past Continuous: Participle + hwā

Placed after a participle, hwā turns the present into a continuous or habitual past. In this use it is enclitic and its He is silent (pronounced wā):

  • ܟܬܒ ܗܘܐ kāteb (h)wā = he was writing, he used to write.
  • ܟܬܒܐ ܗܘܬ kātbā (h)wāt = she was writing.
  • ܟܬܒܝܢ ܗܘܘ kātbīn (h)waw = they were writing.

Placed after a perfect it gives a pluperfect: ܟܬܒ ܗܘܐ ktab (h)wā = he had written. In unpointed text the two look the same, and the context decides.
Which two verbs does the lesson single out as highly irregular?

feedback.text: These are I-Alaph roots, but regular in pattern.
These are I-Yodh roots, not the singled-out pair.

name.text: Module 2 · Lesson 7 · Section 7: The Story — Part 7

questiontext.text:
Section 7: The Story — Part 7

The Summons

Narrative note: The scene returns to the king’s guards, who have heard what Yukhannan said in the temple (Lesson 6). Pay attention to the massive use of weak roots—ʾemar (said), ʾezal (went), ʾīdaʿ (knew), hwā (was/became), ḥzayn (we saw), ʾetā (came).

Sentence 1

ܟܕ ܐܡܪ ܝܘܚܢܢ ܡܠܬܐ ܕܐܠܗܐ ܐܙܠܘ ܢܛܘܪ̈ܐ ܠܘܬ ܡܠܟܐ kad ʾemar Yūḥannan meltā d-ʾAlāhā, ʾezal(w) nāṭōrē lwāt malkā. kad (when) ʾemar (said) Yūḥannan (John) meltā (the-word) d-ʾAlāhā (of-God), ʾezal(w) (went) nāṭōrē (the-guards) lwāt (to-the-presence-of) malkā (the-king). → When Yukhannan said the word of God, the guards went to the king.

Sentence 2

ܐܡܪܝܢ ܠܗ ܝܕܥܝܢ ܚܢܢ ܡܐ ܗܘܐ ܒܗܝܟܠܐ ʾāmrīn leh: yādʿīn ḥnan mā hwā b-hayklā! ʾāmrīn (they-[are]-saying) leh (to-him): yādʿīn (knowing) ḥnan (are-we) mā (what) hwā (happened/was) b-hayklā (in-the-temple)! → They say to him: “We know what happened in the temple!”

Sentence 3

ܚܙܝܢ ܓܒܪܐ ܘܐܡܪ ܡܠܬܐ ܒܝܫܬܐ ḥzayn gabrā, w-ʾemar meltā bīštā. ḥzayn (we-saw) gabrā (a-man), w-ʾemar (and-said) meltā (a-word) bīštā (evil-[f]). → “We saw a man, and he said an evil word.”

Sentence 4

ܗܘܐ ܗܫܐ ܡܠܟܐ ܪܓܝܙ ܛܒ hwā hāšā malkā rgīz ṭāb. hwā (became/was) hāšā (now) malkā (the-king) rgīz (angry) ṭāb (greatly/very). → Now the king was very angry.

Sentence 5

ܐܡܪ ܡܠܟܐ ܠܢܛܘܪ̈ܐ ܐܝܬܐܘܗܝ ܠܗܪܟܐ ʾemar malkā l-nāṭōrē: ʾaytaʾū(hy) l-harkā! ʾemar (said) malkā (the-king) l-nāṭōrē (to-the-guards): ʾaytaʾū(hy) (bring-him! [Aphel imperative m.pl. of ʾ-t-y + 3 m.sg. suffix; imperatives and object suffixes come in Lessons 9 and 11]) l-harkā (to-here)! → The king said to the guards: “Bring him here!”

Sentence 6

ܘܐܬܐ ܝܘܚܢܢ ܩܕܡ ܡܠܟܐ w-ʾetā Yūḥannan qdām malkā. w-ʾetā (and-came) Yūḥannan (John) qdām (before) malkā (the-king). → And Yukhannan came before the king.
In the story, to whom did the guards go?

feedback.text: They went to report on him.
They report what happened in the temple.

questiontext.text: What do the guards claim they saw and heard?

answer.text: A man who said an evil word
A light from God at the gate

feedback.text: The king's anger follows their report.

questiontext.text: How did the king react to the news?

answer.text: He became very angry (rgīz ṭāb) and ordered the man brought to him.
He went to the gate himself.

feedback.text: He has the guards bring Yukhannan.

questiontext.text: In sentence 2, what does yādʿīn ḥnan mean?

feedback.text: The past would be the perfect.

Section 10: Grammatical Summary

WEAK VERB SHIFT SUMMARY

Class Root Shift Rule 3 m.sg Example 1 c.sg Example
I-Alaph ʾ-m-r First vowel becomes e ʾemar (he said) ʾemret (I said)
I-Yodh y-d-ʿ Initial vowelless y → ī ʾīdaʿ (he knew) yedʿet (I knew)
III-Yodh ḥ-z-y Yodh drops, ends in ā in 3ms ḥzā (he saw) ḥzēt (I saw)
Double Weak ʾ-t-y Follows both rules ʾetā (he came) ʾetēt (I came)
Hollow q-w-m Middle radical becomes long ā qām (he rose) qāmet (I rose)
I-Nun n-p-q Perfect regular; n assimilates in imperfect and Aphel npaq (he went out) nepqet (I went out); impf. neppūq
